Joan Robinson introduced the term in *The Economics of Imperfect Competition* as a way to describe buyer power, and the classic textbook example is a firm that is the dominant buyer of labour in an isolated town. Its relevance in economics is that wages may then reflect not only workers’ productivity, but also workers’ limited outside options.\n\nIn labour markets, monopsony need not mean there is literally only one employer. Modern “monopsony” often refers to imperfect competition caused by search frictions, commuting costs, licensing barriers, non-compete clauses, job-specific skills, care responsibilities, immigration constraints, or simple employer concentration. Alan Manning’s *Monopsony in Motion* argues that when workers cannot instantly move to equivalent jobs, firms face an upward-sloping labour supply curve and can set wages below marginal product without losing their entire workforce. This makes monopsony central to debates on minimum wages, antitrust policy, collective bargaining, inequality, and the labour share of income.\n\nPotential examples include hospital systems in local healthcare labour markets, where mergers can reduce outside options for specialized workers. Prager and Schmitt find that hospital mergers slowed wage growth when the merger substantially increased local employer concentration and when workers’ skills were specific to hospitals. Another example is concentrated local hiring in particular occupations: Azar, Marinescu, and Steinbaum show that many U.S. labour markets, defined by occupation and commuting zone, are highly concentrated, suggesting that workers in some places face only a few serious potential employers. More generally, evidence that firms differ in wage-setting power, even for similar workers, links monopsony to wage inequality; Card, Cardoso, Heining, and Kline review evidence that firm-level wage policies matter for inequality, while Azar, Berry, and Marinescu estimate substantial labour-market power using online job-application data. Policy-oriented work by Naidu, Posner, and Weyl therefore treats labour monopsony as an antitrust problem as well as a labour-market problem.\n\nA useful short framing is: monopsony matters because labour markets are often “thin” or frictional, so employers may have discretion over pay. Where workers cannot easily switch jobs, employer concentration, mergers, restrictive contracts, or platform control can suppress wages, reduce mobility, and make employment outcomes differ from the competitive benchmark.\n\n**References**\n\n- Azar, José, Steven T. The best way to start astrophotography is **not** to buy a big telescope first. Start with simple sky photography, learn what targets you enjoy, then choose gear based on that. Astrophotography splits into a few different hobbies: Moon/planets, Milky Way/nightscapes, deep-sky nebulae/galaxies, and solar. They use different equipment.\n\nPrices and availability below are based on current listings I checked on **May 9, 2026**, so treat them as approximate.\n\n**Start With The Cheapest Useful Path**\n\nIf you already have a smartphone or camera, start there.\n\n1. **Shoot the Moon**\n - Use a phone, mirrorless, DSLR, or compact camera.\n - Put it on a tripod or lean it against something stable.\n - Use manual exposure if possible. The Moon is bright, so expose it more like daylight than nighttime.\n - Try different phases. Crescent, quarter, and gibbous phases show crater shadows better than a full Moon.\n\n2. **Shoot Star Trails**\n - Put a camera or phone on a tripod.\n - Take many 10-30 second exposures, then stack them.\n - This teaches focusing, battery management, dew, framing, and patience without expensive gear.\n\n3. **Shoot The Milky Way**\n - Best from darker skies, ideally **Bortle 4 or darker**. Learn interval shooting and stacking.\n\nWeek 3: Milky Way or bright winter/summer constellations \nTry wide-field shots from the darkest place you can reasonably reach.\n\nWeek 4: Stacking and processing \nUse free tools like **Siril**, **DeepSkyStacker**, **Sequator**, **GraXpert**, or **GIMP/Photoshop/Lightroom**. Big Dobsonians are great for visual astronomy but usually awkward for astrophotography.\n- Underestimating the mount. Spend a few nights on the Moon, star trails, and wide-field sky shots. Why does a bad question make discussion keep diffusing without ever progressing? Why do some questions, once clearly stated, almost produce their own method? All of these phenomena suggest that questioning is not merely requesting information from outside; it is in fact organizing a search process. .\en\docs\04-questioning-as-an-algorithm.md:19:But the analogy has limits. For mature problems, such as solving an exercise, proving a lemma, or making a diagnosis, the nodes and branches of the tree are often already clear, and questioning mainly selects a route within them.
